You are helping a user write SQL queries to a database. If something is not clear, you can ask the user to clarify what they need. The schema for the database being accessed is the following:
        
CREATE TABLE battle (
    id INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT,
    date TEXT,
    bulgarian_commander TEXT,
    latin_commander TEXT,
    result TEXT,
    UNIQUE (id)
);

CREATE TABLE ship (
    lost_in_battle INT,
    id INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT,
    tonnage TEXT,
    ship_type TEXT,
    location TEXT,
    disposition_of_ship TEXT,
    UNIQUE (id),
    FOREIGN KEY (lost_in_battle) REFERENCES battle(id)
);

CREATE TABLE death (
    caused_by_ship_id INT,
    id INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    note TEXT,
    killed INT,
    injured INT,
    UNIQUE (id),
    FOREIGN KEY (caused_by_ship_id) REFERENCES ship(id)
);

To list “historical battles” from your database, you can query the `battle` table. Here are a few useful options:

```sql
-- All battles (basic list)
SELECT
  id, name, date, bulgarian_commander, latin_commander, result
FROM battle
ORDER BY date, name;
```

```sql
-- Battles with ships lost (and how many)
SELECT
  b.id,
  b.name,
  b.date,
  COUNT(s.id) AS ships_lost
FROM battle b
JOIN ship s ON s.lost_in_battle = b.id
GROUP BY b.id, b.name, b.date
ORDER BY b.date, b.name;
```

```sql
-- Battles with total killed/injured (from deaths caused by ships in that battle)
SELECT
  b.id,
  b.name,
  b.date,
  COALESCE(SUM(d.killed), 0)  AS total_killed,
  COALESCE(SUM(d.injured), 0) AS total_injured
FROM battle b
LEFT JOIN ship s ON s.lost_in_battle = b.id
LEFT JOIN death d ON d.caused_by_ship_id = s.id
GROUP BY b.id, b.name, b.date
ORDER BY b.date, b.name;
```

Which do you mean by “historical battles”: a simple list, battles with ship losses, or battles with casualties?
I want battles where more than 10 people were killed.

```sql
SELECT
  b.id,
  b.name,
  b.date,
  SUM(d.killed) AS total_killed
FROM battle b
JOIN ship  s ON s.lost_in_battle = b.id
JOIN death d ON d.caused_by_ship_id = s.id
GROUP BY b.id, b.name, b.date
HAVING SUM(d.killed) > 10
ORDER BY total_killed DESC, b.date;
```
make sure total deaths are over 10 for all participants

If you mean **the combined total killed across all ships/participants in the battle** must be > 10, use this (it sums all `death` rows linked to ships in that battle):

```sql
SELECT
  b.id,
  b.name,
  b.date,
  COALESCE(SUM(d.killed), 0) AS total_killed
FROM battle b
LEFT JOIN ship  s ON s.lost_in_battle = b.id
LEFT JOIN death d ON d.caused_by_ship_id = s.id
GROUP BY b.id, b.name, b.date
HAVING COALESCE(SUM(d.killed), 0) > 10
ORDER BY total_killed DESC, b.date;
```

If instead you mean **each participant/ship in the battle must have > 10 killed** (i.e., no ship with 10 or fewer), tell me and I’ll adjust the query.
just make sure to include battle names and IDs too

```sql
SELECT
  b.id,
  b.name,
  COALESCE(SUM(d.killed), 0) AS total_killed
FROM battle b
LEFT JOIN ship  s ON s.lost_in_battle = b.id
LEFT JOIN death d ON d.caused_by_ship_id = s.id
GROUP BY b.id, b.name
HAVING COALESCE(SUM(d.killed), 0) > 10
ORDER BY total_killed DESC, b.id;
```
make sure to get unique IDs for the battles too

`battle.id` is already unique (it’s the PRIMARY KEY). The query below returns one row per battle (unique battle ID) with the battle name:

```sql
SELECT
  b.id AS battle_id,
  b.name AS battle_name,
  COALESCE(SUM(d.killed), 0) AS total_killed
FROM battle b
LEFT JOIN ship  s ON s.lost_in_battle = b.id
LEFT JOIN death d ON d.caused_by_ship_id = s.id
GROUP BY b.id, b.name
HAVING COALESCE(SUM(d.killed), 0) > 10
ORDER BY total_killed DESC, b.id;
```
